nicFW950 v6.00.15e [Release]

nicsure

16. Oktober

!!WARNING!!

DO NOT use the RMS to flash this firmware. Use the Radtel Firmware Flashing Tool or the Web Based Flasher.

⚠️ BEFORE FLASHING CUSTOM FIRMWARE, MAKE SURE YOU HAVE A STORAGE BACKUP ⚠️

Storage Backup Instructions

Community Support

I 'maintain' a Telegram group and Facebook Group specifically for nicFW support and discussion. If you need some help or have a suggestion, by all means pop in and ask. If you're an advanced user, maybe consider hanging around and helping others.

Click Here to go to the 'nicFW Hangout' on Telegram

Click here to visit the nicFW Support page on Facebook

Documentation

nicFW is in Beta stage, meaning I'm focusing on features and bugs tracking, not creating documentation. However, since nicFW950 is mostly identical to nicFW880, the existing documentation Wiki will apply to 95% of operation. Where differences exist, the Wiki will be updated in time. Remember I'm just one guy.

Click Here For The Wiki

It is advised to perform a storage reset after flashing this firmware as critical default settings values have changed.

Instructions for performing a Storage Reset

RMS Downloads are attached below.

I forgot to include the external microphone icon in the RMS' default fonts. You will need the attached 'symbols.rmsfont' file and load it into the RMS before flashing other fonts to prevent losing the external microphone icon.

What is the 'x' version?

If you see a download attached to this release post with an 'x' suffix, this is what I call a preview release. A bit of a misnomer to be honest, but a word is just a word.

When users report bugs or glitches, I work to fix them as quickly as possible. However, these fixes are often made alongside ongoing development, so the resulting firmware may also contain changes, improvements, or experimental features intended for the next full release.

Think of it as going beyond the bleeding edge and well into the bandages!

A little caution is advised when using these versions. They may contain unfinished or untested features, and some settings or functionality may not yet be supported by the RMS.

Updates

  • External microphone/headset support. (Thanks Paul) This means the mics and headsets specifically made for the 950. Do not use any other kind.
    I had to pretty much re-write the audio system to do this, so there may be audio glitches lurking under the bridge.

  • AM/DSB TX has moved to an interrupt driven system.

    WARNING
    AM and DSB TX causes thermal stress to the radio's internal components. This is within the limits of what it was designed to tolerate on standard frequencies such as 11m, 2m and 70cm. But outside of those bands, the heating is in addition to the thermal stress transmitting on those bands causes naturally. This can be enough collectively to cause a shutdown due to overheating. AM TX also generates some wide band splatter, this is unfortunately unavoidable due to how the power output needs to be manipulated to achieve AM. So while AM transmission works, it isn't perfect.

    • Advanced -> AM DSB TX Dp (Depth)
      Defines a normalization clipping window around the TX audio. Smaller windows will give wider audio response, larger windows will give clearer audio. It's a balance.

    • Advanced -> AM DSB MGain (Mic Gain)
      Controls the amplifier gain that processes the microphone audio during AM/DSB TX.

    • Advanced -> AM Envelope
      Sets the Post-Amble of the AM envelope. Larger values result in decreased output power but stronger audio, lower values give higher output power but weaker audio.

    • AM TX SmplFrq (Sample Frequency)
      Sets the sample rate of the TX audio in kHz for AM and DSB. Higher frequencies give better audio clarity but eat more battery power.
      The new interrupt system can cause phase/beating audio artefacts, fine tuning of this setting can eliminate it.

    • DSB Phase Fr (Frequency)
      Sets the frequency shift in dHz used to adjust the RF phase during DSB TX. This is a bit of a hack however, you will need to experiment.

    • The modulation level bar will now work in AM mode. In DSB mode the actual power meter will deflect with audio modulation level.

    • Note that DSB TX is not very good. This is an area I am continuing to experiment with however, but for now it sounds crap.

    • The AM TX warning has been put back. But you only need accept it once.

  • I needed to adjust the timings on channel scanning. As a result, the Channel Scan Speed you have set may feel slightly slower, just knock it up by 2 or 3 if so.

  • Channel scanning speeds of 40 or more use a different scanning technique which is slightly faster. This will also apply to Multiwatch and Groupwatch too if set.

  • The signal floor is now dynamically calculated from actual band conditions.

  • Increased the range and defaults of the FM Deviation settings, as regular FM TX audio on this radio is very quiet at the same levels used for the RT-880.

  • The modulation level bar now operates better visually.

  • Small improvement on battery life.

v6.00.15c

  • Fixed audio ticking glitch in Tuner Mode while Multiwatch is enabled.

  • Dropped the UHF threshold frequency to 200 MHz to allow better performance on 220 MHz

  • AM/DSB Warning only appeared on DSB TX before, it now appears for both. Again it need only be accepted once.

  • Fixed some settings not saving properly on power off due to not performing a settings sync after the setting is changed. I fixed by ensuring a sync occurs just before power-down.

v6.00.15d

  • I hit the 256k flash limit for firmware size, so I had to enable mild optimization. This affected timing and could have knock on effects. I think I've identified all of it though.

  • Increased the Mic Gain setting so its high value is now 63 and changed the default to 48. All deviation settings have been returned to their previous defaults. High TX Deviation causes hum on some radios, so I used another method of boosting TX audio. If you previously had a high TX Deviation, kick it back down to sensible values. Same goes for the Subtone Deviation and APRS Deviation.
    Note: The RMS still caps this to 31 of course. You'll have to live with this until 16b which will have the updated RMS.

  • Returned the UHF split point to 280 MHz (sorry about the 200 MHz debacle on 15c, I was misinformed, other testers confirmed that stock firmware and nicFW [pre 15c] performed the same on 220 MHz). However, this split point may now be set in the Advanced menu.

  • Maurizio Brameri identified a problem with the Storage Reset system, this version does not correctly wipe the radio. It will be fixed for the next build.

v6.00.15e

  • Fixed issue with Storage Reset not working correctly.

  • Menu Shortcuts when linked to a number based menu now open the Main Menu with that item selected.

Oh the bandwidth, sorry I didn't read it properly, my bad. It's deliberately non-functional. bandwidth settings for SSB are very specific and they're hard coded for general reception. If I expose the bandwidth settings to SSB people would change them, forget they've done it, then go posting here that SSB is not working properly. The bandwidth setting adjusts only the Si4732 register that deals with AM reception. SSB bandwidth is different register entirely, so I'd have to make another setting as it can't be the same one as AM which would clutter things, make the UI more confusing and cause many posts about it. IF I share the setting, it would cause the previous problem. My solution to that headache was to just hard code it.

This means it takes 4 consecutive low readings to trigger any low battery related action. The first thing I want to do is get RX audio to stream to the RMS while the remote is active. This is doable, using PortAudio it should work on all platforms too. The scan and record system naturally follows from that. The next goal will be TX audio. This is doable but tricker. Finally, once RX and TX audio can be streamed, this opens up networking. A server system can be connected to the radio and proxy the serial data over a network connection. Then a small remote app on an Android device could connect and fully operate the radio, from anywhere. I have already done this with Quansheng radios, but it was clunky and required an audio interface and a lot of setup. This would be much simpler. Another byproduct of this (if someone could write an Asterisk driver for it) is that a node could use a 950 and require only a USB cable. Anyway, that's the direction this avenue of features will be moving.

An advanced look at how nicFW950 decodes APRS audio, and why having a choice of demodulation methods can make a difference. A Little Background APRS decoding involves several layers and stages, but at its most fundamental level, it all starts with a series of rapidly alternating audible tones. For standard 1200-baud APRS, these tones have two distinct frequencies: 1200 Hz : MARK (the lower-frequency tone) 2200 Hz : SPACE (the higher-frequency tone) The signal operates at 1200 baud , meaning there are 1,200 signalling intervals per second. The tones don't necessarily change every interval, but together they carry the information that eventually becomes an APRS packet. Arguably, one of the most important parts of decoding APRS is this very first stage, known as demodulation . In simple terms, the raw audio is analysed to determine which of the two frequencies is present at any given moment. The result is a stream of MARK and SPACE decisions that can be passed to the subsequent stages of the decoder. It sounds straightforward, but there are quite a few ways to accomplish it! How Do We Detect the Tones? There are numerous approaches to demodulating an audio FSK signal. Your old dial-up modem from the 1980s probably used a dedicated integrated circuit. Feed it an audio signal, and the chip would produce a digital output indicating whether it was detecting a MARK or SPACE. At the other end of the spectrum, Dire Wolf , the popular APRS and packet radio software for PCs, employs sophisticated digital signal processing techniques such as FFT to extract the information from the audio. For a modern PC processor running at 3 GHz or more, this kind of processing is hardly a challenge. The RT-950 Pro , however, is a rather different environment. Its processor is perfectly respectable for an embedded device, running at 200 MHz , but we don't have the luxury of a desktop-class CPU or dedicated hardware for APRS demodulation. Complex signal processing at the required sampling rates can quickly become expensive, particularly when the processor has plenty of other jobs to do. Consequently, nicFW950 needs demodulation algorithms that are not only reliable but also computationally efficient. And this is where things get interesting. Two Different Approaches nicFW950 offers a choice between two fundamentally different demodulation methods: 1. Peak/Valley Detection : A lightweight, time-domain approach that examines the shape of the audio waveform. 2. Goertzel Discrimination : A frequency-domain approach that measures the strength of the two expected tones. Both aim to achieve exactly the same result: identifying MARK and SPACE tones. The difference is how they arrive at that decision. 1. Peak/Valley Detection If you look closely at an audio waveform, you'll notice that it is, wait for it, a wave! It has peaks , where the signal rises to a maximum before beginning to fall, and valleys , where it reaches a minimum before rising again. These points are particularly useful because they represent changes in the direction of the waveform. We can detect them simply by following the incoming audio samples and observing when the signal changes from rising to falling, or vice versa. In effect, we're tracking the waveform's turning points. Why is this useful? A significant advantage of this approach is that it doesn't depend on the audio waveform crossing a fixed voltage threshold. A conventional zero-crossing detector looks for points where the signal passes through zero. Unfortunately, any DC offset or drift in the audio can interfere with that process. Peak/Valley detection is largely insensitive to these offsets because it is interested in changes of direction rather than absolute signal levels. This gives us something considerably more robust than simple zero-crossing detection, while retaining much of its computational efficiency. Turning Peaks into Frequencies Once we can identify these turning points, the next step is to examine how frequently they occur. Consider the two APRS tones: 1200 Hz (MARK): A lower-frequency tone with a longer period, producing fewer peaks and valleys over a given interval. 2200 Hz (SPACE): A higher-frequency tone with a shorter period, producing more peaks and valleys over the same interval. By examining the rate at which these transitions occur, the demodulator can distinguish between the two tones. The result is a MARK or SPACE decision, ready to be passed along to the next stage of the decoder. The big advantage? This technique is extremely lightweight. It requires relatively little mathematical processing, making it particularly attractive for an embedded processor where CPU time and power consumption matter. Of course, there is a trade-off. Noise can introduce additional peaks and valleys into the waveform, potentially confusing the detector and making the two frequencies harder to distinguish. Low pass filtering and transition hysteresis ( two configurable values in the APRS menu ) can however mitigate this to some degree. This is where our second method takes a rather different approach. 2. Goertzel Discrimination Instead of looking at the shape of the waveform and counting its turning points, what if we could directly measure how much of a particular frequency is present? That's essentially what the Goertzel algorithm allows us to do. Goertzel is a digital signal processing technique designed to evaluate the strength of a specific frequency within a collection of audio samples. Rather than calculating an entire frequency spectrum, as a conventional FFT might, it concentrates on just the frequencies we're interested in. For APRS, that makes it particularly convenient because we already know exactly which two frequencies we're looking for. How Does It Work? Imagine taking a short section of incoming audio. Using the Goertzel algorithm, we can calculate a value representing the signal's energy at 1200 Hz . We then perform a similar calculation for 2200 Hz . The algorithm uses a frequency-specific coefficient to perform these calculations efficiently. We now have two values: MARK energy : How strongly the audio contains the 1200 Hz tone. SPACE energy : How strongly the audio contains the 2200 Hz tone. By comparing these values, we can determine which tone is dominant. If the 1200 Hz energy is greater, we have a MARK. If the 2200 Hz energy is greater, we have a SPACE. That decision can then be passed to the next stage of the decoder, just as with Peak/Valley detection with a little hysteresis to filter out indeterminate readings at the transition points. So What's the Catch? Although Goertzel is an efficient way of detecting specific frequencies, it still requires considerably more mathematical processing than simply tracking peaks and valleys. Each incoming audio sample contributes to calculations for both target frequencies, and the resulting energy measurements must be evaluated over suitable sampling intervals. On a desktop PC, this kind of workload is trivial. On a 200 MHz embedded processor that's also managing the radio, user interface, and numerous other tasks, the difference becomes much more relevant. The potential benefit is improved discrimination when the received audio contains noise or unwanted signal components, but at the cost of battery life. By concentrating on the energy at the two expected frequencies, Goertzel may be better able to distinguish the wanted tones from some forms of interference. However, this isn't a universal guarantee. Performance depends on the nature of the noise, signal quality, sampling strategy, and implementation. 3. Peak/Valley vs Goertzel, Which Is Better? That's the interesting question, and unfortunately, there isn't a definitive answer. Both methods have strengths and weaknesses. Peak/Valley detection has a clear advantage when it comes to computational efficiency. Less processing means less CPU activity devoted to demodulation, which can contribute to improved battery life. Goertzel, on the other hand, offers a potentially more selective method of detecting the wanted frequencies, particularly when the received signal is less than ideal. But radio signals rarely behave perfectly, and what works best under one set of conditions won't necessarily perform better under another. A strong, clean APRS signal might decode equally well using either method. A weak or noisy signal could favour one approach over the other, depending on the characteristics of the interference. And that's precisely why nicFW950 offers both. 4. Why Give Users the Choice? One of the design philosophies behind nicFW is to give users as much control as reasonably possible. Rather than deciding that one demodulation technique is universally superior, I've made both available so you can experiment and decide which works best for your particular conditions. If you're receiving APRS packets reliably, there's probably little reason to change anything. But if decoding performance isn't quite what you'd expect, switching demodulation methods gives you another variable to experiment with. You might find that Goertzel handles a particularly noisy environment more effectively. Alternatively, Peak/Valley might deliver equally good results while consuming fewer processor resources. The important thing is that you have the choice. Of course, offering more options inevitably introduces a little more complexity. That's always the balancing act with firmware like nicFW. More flexibility means more settings, more possibilities, and occasionally more things to experiment with! But I'd rather provide the tools and let you decide how best to use them. Final Thoughts Demodulation is only the first step in decoding an APRS packet, but it's a critical one. Everything that follows depends on accurately recovering the information contained in those two audio tones. Peak/Valley and Goertzel take very different routes to achieve that goal, and each brings its own advantages. Neither method is guaranteed to outperform the other in every situation, which makes having both available genuinely useful. So, if you're curious about what happens beneath the surface when nicFW950 receives an APRS packet, or you're looking to squeeze a little more performance out of your setup, try experimenting with the demodulation setting. And if you do notice a consistent improvement with one method over the other, I'd be interested to hear about it! As always, the aim with nicFW is to provide flexibility without unnecessarily sacrificing performance. Sometimes that means giving you a few more knobs to twiddle. Happy experimenting!

If you see a download attached to this release post with an 'x' suffix , this is what I call a preview release. A bit of a misnomer to be honest, but a word is just a word. When users report bugs or glitches, I work to fix them as quickly as possible. However, these fixes are often made alongside ongoing development, so the resulting firmware may also contain changes, improvements, or experimental features intended for the next full release. Think of it as going beyond the bleeding edge and well into the bandages! A little caution is advised when using these versions. They may contain unfinished or untested features, and some settings or functionality may not yet be supported by the RMS . Updates External microphone/headset support . ( Thanks Paul ) This means the mics and headsets specifically made for the 950. Do not use any other kind. I had to pretty much re-write the audio system to do this, so there may be audio glitches lurking under the bridge. AM/DSB TX has moved to an interrupt driven system. WARNING AM and DSB TX causes thermal stress to the radio's internal components. This is within the limits of what it was designed to tolerate on standard frequencies such as 11m, 2m and 70cm. But outside of those bands, the heating is in addition to the thermal stress transmitting on those bands causes naturally. This can be enough collectively to cause a shutdown due to overheating. AM TX also generates some wide band splatter, this is unfortunately unavoidable due to how the power output needs to be manipulated to achieve AM. So while AM transmission works, it isn't perfect. Advanced -> AM DSB TX Dp (Depth) Defines a normalization clipping window around the TX audio. Smaller windows will give wider audio response, larger windows will give clearer audio. It's a balance. Advanced -> AM DSB MGain (Mic Gain) Controls the amplifier gain that processes the microphone audio during AM/DSB TX. Advanced -> AM Envelope Sets the Post-Amble of the AM envelope. Larger values result in decreased output power but stronger audio, lower values give higher output power but weaker audio. AM TX SmplFrq (Sample Frequency) Sets the sample rate of the TX audio in kHz for AM and DSB. Higher frequencies give better audio clarity but eat more battery power. The new interrupt system can cause phase/beating audio artefacts, fine tuning of this setting can eliminate it. DSB Phase Fr (Frequency) Sets the frequency shift in dHz used to adjust the RF phase during DSB TX . This is a bit of a hack however, you will need to experiment. The modulation level bar will now work in AM mode. In DSB mode the actual power meter will deflect with audio modulation level. Note that DSB TX is not very good. This is an area I am continuing to experiment with however, but for now it sounds crap. The AM TX warning has been put back. But you only need accept it once. I needed to adjust the timings on channel scanning . As a result, the Channel Scan Speed you have set may feel slightly slower, just knock it up by 2 or 3 if so. Channel scanning speeds of 40 or more use a different scanning technique which is slightly faster. This will also apply to Multiwatch and Groupwatch too if set. The signal floor is now dynamically calculated from actual band conditions. Increased the range and defaults of the FM Deviation settings, as regular FM TX audio on this radio is very quiet at the same levels used for the RT-880. The modulation level bar now operates better visually. Small improvement on battery life. v6.00.15c Fixed audio ticking glitch in Tuner Mode while Multiwatch is enabled. Dropped the UHF threshold frequency to 200 MHz to allow better performance on 2 20 MHz AM/DSB Warning only appeared on DSB TX before, it now appears for both. Again it need only be accepted once. Fixed some settings not saving properly on power off due to not performing a settings sync after the setting is changed. I fixed by ensuring a sync occurs just before power-down. v6.00.15d I hit the 256k flash limit for firmware size, so I had to enable mild optimization. This affected timing and could have knock on effects. I think I've identified all of it though. Increased the Mic Gain setting so its high value is now 63 and changed the default to 48 . All deviation settings have been returned to their previous defaults. High TX Deviation causes hum on some radios, so I used another method of boosting TX audio. If you previously had a high TX Deviation , kick it back down to sensible values. Same goes for the Subtone Deviation and APRS Deviation . Note: The RMS still caps this to 31 of course. You'll have to live with this until 16b which will have the updated RMS . Returned the UHF split point to 280 MHz ( sorry about the 200 MHz debacle on 15c, I was misinformed, other testers confirmed that stock firmware and nicFW [pre 15c] performed the same on 220 MHz ). However, this split point may now be set in the Advanced menu. Maurizio Brameri identified a problem with the Storage Reset system, this version does not correctly wipe the radio. It will be fixed for the next build. v6.00.15e Fixed issue with Storage Reset not working correctly. Menu Shortcuts when linked to a number based menu now open the Main Menu with that item selected. BETA STATUS Most of the bugs found during the initial porting work have now been addressed, so I'm moving the firmware into the Beta stage . There are still areas being actively developed and tested, but the core port is now at the point where wider testing makes sense. AM TRANSMIT EXPERIMENT The AM transmit experiment is included in this release. It's still very much experimental. At the moment it doesn't perform particularly well at higher power settings, and the audio can sound a little scratchy. I'll continue working on improving it. The documentation has been updated with the relevant settings and explanations: https://github.com/nicsure/RMS880/wiki/Advanced-Menu#am-emulation-notes ⚠️ IMPORTANT AM transmit has not been soak tested , so there is a possibility of hardware damage. Please only experiment with this feature if you are comfortable accepting that risk. I'll continue testing it myself to see whether my radio eventually pops its clogs , so if you're not comfortable with the risk, you may wish to wait until I have more data. The later versions from 10b onward use a different method of AM generation that is far less likely to cause hardware issues. You cannot accidentally transmit in AM . A warning screen is displayed before AM transmit can be enabled. The RT-880 cannot use this method because of differences in its audio routing, so unfortunately this feature cannot be backported to the 880 . FOCUS MODE UPDATE When using Focus Mode, you can now stretch the VFO fonts to double height . Set: Advanced → Font Double → On Also, when you're in a channel or group setup, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which VFO is currently selected. The main icon bar now displays a I, II or III indicator showing which VFO is selected. CROSS-BAND REPEATER Cross-Band Repeater is now implemented. It works in the same way as the 880 version, with the addition of a monitoring function . The monitoring function is not possible on the 880 because of its different audio routing, so this part cannot be backported. v6.00.10b Update Continue to use RMS v6.00.09b with this until I can release an update to the RMS later. AM Transmit Improved significantly. Note: The ' AM TX Period' setting now does nothing. Only 'AM TX Depth' is relevant now. Smart Scan List is now persistent. User function 'Clr SmrtScan' added to clear the Smart Scan List. Fixed issue with LEFT button in channel mode. VFO Scans will now display a channel name if the scan frequency matches a stored channel. Added user function 'Ignore GW-CH' to exclude a nuisance channel from GroupWatch Default Key: SP-# Note: Previous settings will prevent the default key being applied, best to perform a Storage Reset anyway. v6.00.11b Update Keep using RMS v6.00.09b for now, I'll get the new RMS out soon. A Storage Reset is recommended. Tightened AM TX Audio on lower power settings. Changed AM receive method for HF frequencies. Re-introduced ' AM AGC Fix' in the 'Advanced' menu. Although I don't think it's needed anymore I added it back just in case. Added 'Ignore GroupWatch Channel' user function. Added 'RF-Gain' user function for the ARDF guys. When toggled on, AGC is disabled and a stepped bar icon appears to show RF-Gain is on manual. The noise bar will change to show the level of RF-Gain. Use the rotary encoder to alter the gain level. Note: With no AGC, strong signals can cause RX overload. Added 'Bandwidth' user function. VFO Scan will now display a channel name if the frequency matches a stored channel. 6.00.11x Update A few adjustments to the AM transmission system. Added a couple more fine tuning options in the advanced menu. AM Mic Gain Sets the level of microphone amplification for AM only. AM Envelope There are four preset envelopes (0 to 3). Select which one sounds best for you. AM Depth Sets the clipping window of the ADC audio capture. Lower values will produce more modulation but may introduce distortion if the microphone audio is too loud. APRS Problems still to resolve APRS needs to be handled a little differently on the RT-950-Pro because its audio system works differently from the RT-880. To decode APRS, the MCU needs to sample the received audio through an ADC. On both radios, this ADC is connected to the line-level audio output. There are also two controls that affect the audio: AMP_ENABLE – turns the audio amplifier on or off. AUDIO_MUTE – mutes the audio output. This is also used by the normal squelch system, and can sometimes be referred to as the SQUELCH_GATE . The important difference is how AUDIO_MUTE behaves on the two radios. On the RT-880 , muting the audio does not stop the ADC from receiving the audio signal. This means APRS can work alongside the normal squelch system without any special handling. When an APRS packet is received, the squelch can remain closed, muting the speaker, while the ADC can still receive the audio needed to decode the packet. The RT-950-Pro works differently. When AUDIO_MUTE is enabled, it completely removes the audio signal from the ADC as well. So if the squelch is closed, the APRS decoder has nothing to sample. For the RT-950-Pro, we therefore have to do the opposite: open the audio path so the ADC can receive the APRS signal . The problem is that this would also send the loud, unpleasant APRS tones to the speaker. The solution is to keep the audio path open for the ADC, but switch AMP_ENABLE off so the speaker remains silent. So, unlike the RT-880, APRS on the RT-950-Pro needs its own audio-handling logic: the squelch gate must be opened to allow the ADC to receive the packet, while the amplifier must be disabled to prevent the APRS tones from being heard. It's a relatively small hardware difference, but it means APRS can't simply use the normal squelch behaviour on the RT-950-Pro. macOS bundle https://github.com/nicsure/nicfw950-rms-builder/releases/tag/v6.00.07d
